meta.blurb: Maya buys a battered guitar and tells herself she has no talent. Her teacher Ines, in a small room above a bakery, says everyone starts badly. Over one year Maya learns what practice does to the brain, and what mistakes are for.
meta.bible: Maya: a woman of about thirty-five who learns the Guitar as an adult, and the main character. Ines: her patient Guitar teacher, who teaches in a small room above a Bakery. Theo: Maya's older brother, aged forty, who learns Portuguese. Priya: Maya's friend, who learns the Guitar quickly. Nell: Theo's daughter, aged seven. Setting: Dunmere, a small town, over about one year, from one January to the next. Ines teaches in a room above Alder's Bakery. Walter: Ines's oldest student, seventy-three, who took up the Guitar two years ago. Ana: Theo's wife, born in Portugal, and Nell's mother. Joss: the friend whose party goes badly for Maya. Colm: Maya's manager at the delivery company where she works as a planner. Dev: a kind, calm colleague. Maya's notebook has a Staircase page and a list of mistakes with their fixes. Maya records herself on her phone on Day 31 and listens again a year later. Maya's favourite slow folk song is The Water Is Wide. She performs at Ines's December evening in the room above the Bakery. Key terms: Callus, Calluses, Staircase, Dunmere, Alder, Colm, Ana, Joss, Walter, Dev, Spotlight, Retrieval, Guitar, Chord, Chords, Brain, Brains, Plateau, Feedback, Spotlight, Portuguese, Consolidate, Landing, Metronome. The science is real and hedged: the brain keeps changing through life, spaced practice and self-testing help memory, sleep helps learning, and where something is uncertain the book says so. Voice: warm, honest and practical, never boastful. Each beat teaches one clear idea about how people learn.

beats.scene: Maya carries a battered second-hand guitar up the steps to her flat
beats.summary: Maya buys an old guitar but tells herself that she is not musical.

beats.scene: A street musician plays outside a railway station while commuters hurry past
beats.summary: Two weeks earlier a street musician made Maya want to play.

beats.scene: A cluttered second-hand shop where an old guitar hangs on the wall
beats.summary: Maya buys a second-hand guitar for forty pounds.

beats.scene: Maya sits on her bed frowning at the guitar's six strings
beats.summary: The belief that she is not musical is a story she tells, not a tested fact.

beats.scene: A child in a school hall mouths the words while others sing
beats.summary: A single remark at school had turned into a lifelong belief.

beats.scene: Maya stands at the back of a party while friends sing around a table
beats.summary: The belief had quietly shaped her choices for years.

beats.scene: Maya writes I am not musical on a notepad and looks at it
beats.summary: A belief about ourselves is a story until we test it.

beats.scene: Maya turns a tuning peg while a phone app shows a wobbling needle
beats.summary: Her first small win is tuning the guitar with a free phone app.

beats.scene: A handwritten card on a bakery noticeboard offers guitar lessons for adults
beats.summary: Maya finds a card offering guitar lessons for adults.

beats.scene: Maya types a message on her phone with her thumb hovering over send
beats.summary: Maya books a first lesson and treats it as an experiment.

beats.scene: Maya walks toward a bakery at dusk with the guitar case on her back
beats.summary: On Thursday evening Maya walks to the bakery, nervous and half hoping to turn back.

beats.scene: A narrow staircase beside a bakery door, with the smell of warm bread
beats.summary: The smell of bread and a steep staircase lead to a small room.

beats.scene: Ines, a grey-haired woman in a green cardigan, welcomes Maya with a handshake
beats.summary: Ines asks why Maya wants to learn, and Maya confesses that she is not musical.

beats.scene: Ines adjusts Maya's arm and shoulder around the guitar's curved body
beats.summary: Ines shows Maya how to sit and hold the guitar.

beats.scene: Maya presses a string with her fingertip and winces at a dull thud
beats.summary: At the first lesson Maya's fingers hurt and the sound is awful.

beats.scene: Maya examines her sore fingertips under a lamp while Ines smiles
beats.summary: Sore fingertips are the skin adapting, which shows that the body changes with use.

beats.scene: Ines smiles and holds out a worn page of beginner exercises
beats.summary: Ines says everyone starts badly and that skill is built step by step.

beats.scene: A worn page of exercises covered in pencil marks from many students
beats.summary: Ines gives Maya a worn page of exercises that many students have used.

beats.scene: Ines writes three small tasks on a card for Maya to take home
beats.summary: Ines sets three small tasks for the week instead of one huge one.

beats.scene: Maya walks home past the closing bakery, the guitar on her back
beats.summary: Maya sees that being bad at the start does not mean she is not musical.

beats.scene: A drawing of a brain with glowing paths running between its parts
beats.summary: The brain keeps changing through life, so it is not fixed.

beats.scene: A chalk drawing of the same brain reshaping itself with new glowing lines
beats.summary: Scientists now know that the brain keeps reshaping itself throughout life.

beats.scene: A tiny cell with long branches reaching toward many other cells
beats.summary: The brain is made of billions of cells that connect to each other.

beats.scene: A faint path across a meadow grows wider as walkers cross it
beats.summary: Connections that are used often become stronger, which is why practice works.

beats.scene: A London taxi weaves through narrow streets while a driver studies a map
beats.summary: A famous study of taxi drivers suggests that learning can change the brain.

beats.scene: A man throws three balls in the air in a sunny room
beats.summary: Adults who learned to juggle showed small changes in their brains.

beats.scene: Maya sits cross-legged on a rug, concentrating on one finger on a string
beats.summary: Practice changes the brain only when the practice is careful and focused.

beats.scene: Maya's finger lands exactly on the right fret and the note rings clearly
beats.summary: A single clean note gives Maya her first small evidence of change.

beats.scene: Maya and her brother Theo talk over cups of tea at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Some people start with advantages, but the starting point does not decide the end.

beats.scene: Maya draws a green field with a thin line across it in her notebook
beats.summary: Maya treats each day of practice as one more walk along the path.

beats.scene: Maya presses three fingers on the strings while one string buzzes
beats.summary: At home one chord buzzes however many times she tries it.

beats.scene: Maya leaves the guitar on the bed and runs the tap in the kitchen
beats.summary: Maya nearly gives up, and the old voice returns.

beats.scene: Maya holds her left hand close to her eyes above the guitar neck
beats.summary: Maya looks closely at her hand and finds a finger touching the wrong string.

beats.scene: Maya's fingertip rests on its very tip, close to the metal fret
beats.summary: Maya fixes the buzz by moving her finger and learns a small lesson.

beats.scene: A page with the word buzz circled and an arrow pointing to a finger
beats.summary: A mistake is information: it shows what to fix.

beats.scene: Maya stands at a half-open door with the guitar in her hands
beats.summary: Fear of looking foolish makes people avoid new things.

beats.scene: A crowd of faces turned toward a person who is about to speak
beats.summary: Everyone looks foolish at first, and the fear costs more than the foolishness.

beats.scene: Maya opens the bedroom door and carries the guitar into the sunny living room
beats.summary: Maya brings the guitar out and decides to be seen as a beginner.

beats.scene: Ines points to the word buzz that Maya pencilled on the exercise page
beats.summary: Ines welcomes mistakes and asks Maya to bring her hardest problems.

beats.scene: A notebook page with three columns headed What happened, Why, and Fix
beats.summary: Maya starts a mistake list in her notebook with a cause and a fix for each.

beats.scene: Maya plays a few notes for Theo, who claps and smiles
beats.summary: Maya plays for Theo, who tells her she is gifted.

beats.scene: Maya sits alone, smiling, then frowns as a small worry appears
beats.summary: Praise for talent feels good but sets a quiet trap.

beats.scene: Ines points to a pencil mark on a page where Maya practised
beats.summary: Ines praises how Maya practised, not some supposed gift.

beats.scene: Two columns on a page headed Talent and Practice with small drawings
beats.summary: Praise for effort and method seems to help people keep trying, according to some studies.

beats.scene: Maya draws a line down a page and writes two headings
beats.summary: Maya sees two ways of thinking about ability: fixed, or growing.

beats.scene: Maya writes two dates and two short lines in a notebook
beats.summary: Compare yourself with your own past, not with other people.

beats.scene: Maya watches a famous guitarist on a phone and feels small
beats.summary: A famous guitarist makes Maya feel hopeless.

beats.scene: A drawing of an iceberg with a small tip above the waterline
beats.summary: The expert's skill was built from years of unseen practice.

beats.scene: Maya props her phone on a pile of books and presses record
beats.summary: Maya records herself so that she can compare with her own past.

beats.scene: Maya listens to her first recording and winces, then smiles
beats.summary: Maya listens to her first recording and decides to keep it for a year.

beats.scene: A stretched rubber band between two hands at a wooden table
beats.summary: Learning happens when a task is a little beyond what you can already do.

beats.scene: Ines sets a slightly harder piece on the music stand
beats.summary: Ines chooses a piece that is a little harder than the last.

beats.scene: Maya frowns at a hard page but keeps her fingers on the strings
beats.summary: Feeling that something is hard does not mean you are failing.

beats.scene: A stopwatch beside Maya's hands as she changes between two chords
beats.summary: Maya counts her chord changes and sees real progress.

beats.scene: Maya sits with her chin on her hand, the guitar on her knee
beats.summary: In week five Maya feels that she is no longer improving.

beats.scene: A guitar case closed and standing in the corner of a room
beats.summary: Maya leaves the guitar in its case for three days.

beats.scene: A drawing of a staircase with long flat landings between the steps
beats.summary: Progress comes in steps with flat stretches between, and plateaus are normal.

beats.scene: Ines taps the staircase drawing, then a metronome on the shelf
beats.summary: A plateau can mean the brain is consolidating, or that practice has become too comfortable.

beats.scene: Maya writes the word landing beside several dates in her notebook
beats.summary: Maya marks flat days in her notebook as landings, not failures.

beats.scene: Maya changes chords smoothly while sunlight crosses the music stand
beats.summary: After weeks of no progress, a difficult chord change suddenly works.

beats.scene: Two small goals written on a card pinned to a wall
beats.summary: Small, clear goals work better than a vague wish to be good.

beats.scene: Maya ticks off the first goal on the card with a green pen
beats.summary: A clear goal lets you see whether you have reached it.

beats.scene: A metronome ticks slowly beside Maya's hand on the strings
beats.summary: Practising slowly and carefully is the way to become fast.

beats.scene: Maya plays a bar again and again, the metronome notch moving up one step
beats.summary: Slow, accurate practice builds the right habit before speed is added.

beats.scene: A wall clock shows twenty minutes while Maya plays on a sofa
beats.summary: Short, regular sessions work better than one long session.

beats.scene: A calendar with a small cross marked on each day of a week
beats.summary: Spreading practice over several days helps people remember more.

beats.scene: Maya sleeps peacefully with the guitar resting against the wall nearby
beats.summary: Sleep helps the brain store what was learned during the day.

beats.scene: Maya plays with the music sheet turned face down on the table
beats.summary: Testing yourself from memory helps you learn more than rereading.

beats.scene: A page of music read over and over, beside a closed notebook
beats.summary: Rereading feels easy but teaches less than trying to remember.

beats.scene: A practice card listing five short steps taped to the music stand
beats.summary: Maya builds a short practice routine from everything she has learned.

beats.scene: Theo studies a Portuguese book at his kitchen table with a mug of coffee
beats.summary: Theo is learning Portuguese at forty so that he can talk to his wife's mother.

beats.scene: Ana's mother smiles kindly across a lunch table as Theo speaks
beats.summary: Theo keeps making mistakes in Portuguese, but does not stop.

beats.scene: Maya and Theo compare notebooks across a table
beats.summary: Adults can learn new things well, with some real advantages over children.

beats.scene: A child and an adult stand side by side, each holding a book
beats.summary: Adults and children each have advantages when they learn.

beats.scene: An elderly man in a cardigan sits on the bakery stairs with a guitar
beats.summary: Maya meets Walter, seventy-three, who took up the guitar two years ago.

beats.scene: Walter plays a slow tune on the stairs while Maya listens, smiling
beats.summary: Walter plays slowly but proudly, showing that age is not a wall.

beats.scene: A page where Maya crosses out three words and writes new ones above them
beats.summary: Changing the words she uses about herself changes what she tries next.

beats.scene: Maya writes a long list of things she would like to learn
beats.summary: Many people stop learning because they believe they are too old or too busy.

beats.scene: Theo stirs a pot at the stove and talks to himself in Portuguese
beats.summary: Theo practises by speaking his new language aloud in daily life.

beats.scene: Ana's mother leans forward at a dinner table as Theo speaks slowly
beats.summary: Theo understands a whole sentence from Ana's mother and is delighted.

beats.scene: Ines leans over Maya's shoulder and points at a hand position
beats.summary: Asking for feedback shows you what you cannot see yourself.

beats.scene: A person looks into a mirror at a small smudge on their own cheek
beats.summary: We feel what we meant to do, so we often cannot see what we really did.

beats.scene: A phone propped on a pile of books films Maya's hands on the strings
beats.summary: Maya films her own hands and learns from watching herself.

beats.scene: Ines writes a single comment in pencil at the top of a page
beats.summary: Good feedback is specific, soon and about the next step.

beats.scene: Maya reads a page of notes with a small, steady smile
beats.summary: Criticism is about the work, not about the worth of the person.

beats.scene: Maya walks quickly along a street, a folded page of notes in her hand
beats.summary: Feedback can still sting, and it helps to wait before answering.

beats.scene: Walter stops on the stairs and watches Maya play with his head tilted
beats.summary: Different people notice different things, so it helps to ask more than one.

beats.scene: A man at a pub waves his glass and speaks loudly while Maya listens
beats.summary: Not all advice is good, so sort it by who gives it and why.

beats.scene: Theo with a heart and Ines with a pencil, drawn side by side
beats.summary: Kind praise and honest correction both have a place.

beats.scene: A yellow sticky note with the word thumb stuck on a guitar
beats.summary: Fixing a habit feels strange at first because the old way feels natural.

beats.scene: Joss holds out an invitation card with a guitar drawn in one corner
beats.summary: Maya's friend Joss invites her to a party and asks her to play.

beats.scene: Maya plays in a crowded living room at a friend's party
beats.summary: At the party Maya plays badly in front of friends and feels ashamed.

beats.scene: Friends laugh and chat in a bright room while Maya sits in a corner
beats.summary: Afterwards Maya sits alone and feels sure that everyone saw her fail.

beats.scene: Maya walks home alone in the rain with her guitar case on her back
beats.summary: Walking home, Maya replays the evening and decides she is not a musician after all.

beats.scene: Ines and Maya sit with a pot of tea between them
beats.summary: Ines asks Maya what she actually remembers about the evening.

beats.scene: Maya talks to Joss at his front door the day after the party
beats.summary: The next day Joss barely remembers how Maya played.

beats.scene: A bright lamp shines on one person while others look away
beats.summary: People tend to overestimate how much others notice their mistakes.

beats.scene: Maya writes a list titled What went wrong in her notebook
beats.summary: The real problem was not talent but a lack of rehearsal in front of people.

beats.scene: Ines tells a story with her hands as Maya laughs
beats.summary: Ines shares her own early failure and urges Maya to be as kind to herself as to a friend.

beats.scene: Maya plays quietly in her living room on a Friday evening, no audience
beats.summary: Maya picks up the guitar again and treats the party as one bad evening.

beats.scene: Maya's friend Priya plays a quick tune while Maya watches closely
beats.summary: Maya's friend Priya learns very fast, and Maya feels a sting of envy.

beats.scene: Maya sits alone in the kitchen after Priya has left, frowning at a mug
beats.summary: Maya feels envy and is ashamed of feeling it.

beats.scene: Maya writes the word envy at the top of a page
beats.summary: Envy can show what you want, and it can be turned into a question.

beats.scene: Maya and Priya sit side by side with their guitars, talking
beats.summary: Priya had a head start: she played the violin as a child.

beats.scene: Priya's lunch break: a sandwich beside a guitar on a park bench
beats.summary: Priya's speed also came from regular hours of practice.

beats.scene: Two runners on a track at different speeds, both smiling
beats.summary: People learn at different speeds, but learning is not a race.

beats.scene: Priya explains a chord chart while Maya shows her notebook
beats.summary: The friends agree to swap what each knows.

beats.scene: A metronome ticks beside Priya, whose fingers rush ahead of the beat
beats.summary: Priya also has weak spots, and nobody is simply the talented one.

beats.scene: A map with a route marked, and a ruler lying unused beside it
beats.summary: Other people are better used as a map than as a ruler.

beats.scene: Maya and Priya play the same two chords together, laughing, slightly out of time
beats.summary: The two friends play a messy duet and enjoy it.

beats.scene: Maya shows seven-year-old Nell how to hold a chord shape
beats.summary: Teaching someone else a chord helps Maya understand it better.

beats.scene: Nell frowns at the strings with her finger raised and her mouth open
beats.summary: Nell asks questions that Maya cannot answer, and they decide to find out.

beats.scene: Maya tries to explain a chord and stops, searching for the right words
beats.summary: Teaching exposes the gaps in what we think we know.

beats.scene: Maya explains a chord aloud to a houseplant on her windowsill
beats.summary: Explaining something aloud, even to nobody, strengthens understanding.

beats.scene: Maya tilts her head as a sad chord rings in a quiet room
beats.summary: Curiosity about why things work makes learning stronger.

beats.scene: Ines draws two chords with one note changed between them on a whiteboard
beats.summary: A minor chord differs from a major chord by one lowered note.

beats.scene: Maya turns a tuning peg while the thick string sounds low and slack
beats.summary: Thicker, looser, longer strings give lower notes.

beats.scene: A notebook page headed Why? with a list of questions and small answers
beats.summary: Asking a question first makes the answer stick better.

beats.scene: Nell laughs as her small fingers fail to reach the chord
beats.summary: Nell is bad at the guitar and entirely happy about it.

beats.scene: Nell looks up at Maya with a serious face, her hands on the guitar
beats.summary: Nell asks if Maya is good, and Maya gives an honest answer.

beats.scene: Maya hums a slow folk tune while walking in a park
beats.summary: Maya chooses a slow folk song to learn all the way through.

beats.scene: Maya watches a video, reads a book and plays, all on one desk
beats.summary: There are many ways to learn, and she can use several of them.

beats.scene: Maya looks at a poster listing several learning styles and shakes her head
beats.summary: The idea that each person has one learning style has little support, but mixing methods helps.

beats.scene: Maya hums the tune and plays it by ear, one finger on the strings
beats.summary: Playing by ear is another way to learn, with its own mistakes.

beats.scene: Maya follows a chord chart with one finger above a single line
beats.summary: A chord chart shows her the pattern of the song.

beats.scene: Maya turns her sheet music around on a stand and tries a new way
beats.summary: When stuck, change the method, not the goal.

beats.scene: Maya plays the last bar of a song first, then the one before it
beats.summary: Learning the end of a piece first means every practice finishes on a success.

beats.scene: Maya studies her practice notes beside a guitar and a pencil
beats.summary: Effort alone is not enough; effort needs good strategy and feedback.

beats.scene: Three cards labelled with chords are shuffled on a table
beats.summary: Mixing different skills in one session can help learning, even though it feels harder.

beats.scene: Maya plays The Water Is Wide from start to finish by candlelight
beats.summary: Maya plays the whole song, wobbly but complete, and feels joy.

beats.scene: Maya rests on a sofa under a blanket, the guitar on a chair
beats.summary: After a bad week Maya is too tired to learn anything.

beats.scene: A bedside clock shows midnight while a person lies awake with a phone
beats.summary: Tired minds learn badly, and lack of sleep hurts attention and memory.

beats.scene: Maya sleeps deeply under a blanket with the curtains drawn
beats.summary: Maya skips practice, sleeps, and plays better the next day.

beats.scene: A kitchen timer and a cup of tea beside a guitar
beats.summary: Short breaks inside a practice session help the mind to stay fresh.

beats.scene: Maya walks along a river path at sunrise with headphones on
beats.summary: Exercise and good habits help the brain work well.

beats.scene: A plain breakfast of bread, fruit and water on a sunlit table
beats.summary: Ordinary habits matter more than any special food for the brain.

beats.scene: A dark storm cloud above a small figure who breathes slowly
beats.summary: Too much pressure can narrow thinking, while calm helps learning.

beats.scene: Maya sits with her eyes closed and one hand on her stomach, breathing
beats.summary: Slow breathing can help to calm the body before a hard moment.

beats.scene: Maya plays the same bar twice, once with tense shoulders and once relaxed
beats.summary: The same hard bar is easier when she is calm than when she is tense.

beats.scene: A weekly calendar with one day shaded in soft blue marked rest
beats.summary: Maya makes rest, movement and practice into one balanced week.

beats.scene: Ines holds out a small handwritten invitation for a December evening
beats.summary: Ines invites Maya to play at her small winter evening in four weeks.

beats.scene: Maya stands at the window above the bakery, watching rain run down the glass
beats.summary: Maya remembers the party and hesitates before she answers.

beats.scene: Ines counts on her fingers the differences between the party and the evening
beats.summary: Ines explains that this time there will be preparation, a small friendly audience and a plan.

beats.scene: Maya says yes while Ines writes the date in a small notebook
beats.summary: Maya says yes, and decides to treat the evening as an experiment.

beats.scene: Maya writes a date on a calendar and circles it with a pen
beats.summary: Maya writes the date on a calendar and plans backwards from it.

beats.scene: Maya picks a bar of music with a pencil behind her ear
beats.summary: Maya chooses to play The Water Is Wide and starts with the hardest bars.

beats.scene: Maya plays the song again and again with a pencil behind her ear
beats.summary: Maya works on the hard bars and then plays the whole song without stopping.

beats.scene: Maya deliberately plays a wrong note and carries on with the song
beats.summary: Maya practises making a mistake on purpose and carrying on.

beats.scene: Maya plays for Walter, then Theo, then Nell, then a room of friends
beats.summary: Maya plays for bigger and bigger audiences in small steps.

beats.scene: Walter, with trembling hands, whispers to Maya in the stairwell
beats.summary: Walter says that even at seventy-three he still feels nervous, and that nerves mean it matters.

beats.scene: Maya packs a bag with a spare string, a tuner and water
beats.summary: The day before, Maya packs carefully and rests instead of cramming.

beats.scene: Candles glow on windowsills in the small room above the bakery
beats.summary: On the evening, the small room is full of candles and friendly faces.

beats.scene: Walter plays a slow tune in the candlelight while others watch
beats.summary: The other students play first, which shows Maya that everyone is nervous.

beats.scene: Ines smiles and nods at Maya, who stands with her guitar in the candlelight
beats.summary: It is Maya's turn, and her hands are a little unsteady.

beats.scene: Maya plays the first notes of a slow folk song in candlelight
beats.summary: The first bars come out well.

beats.scene: Maya plays in a candlelit room, her hands a little unsteady
beats.summary: She makes a mistake in the middle of the song and keeps going.

beats.scene: Maya takes a breath and carries on playing without stopping
beats.summary: She does not stop, and the music closes over the mistake.

beats.scene: The audience claps warmly while Maya lowers her guitar and smiles
beats.summary: She finishes the song, the audience applauds, and Maya feels joy and relief.

beats.scene: A woman in a green scarf speaks to Maya while others chat around them
beats.summary: Nobody mentions the wrong note, and Maya's body buzzes with leftover energy.

beats.scene: Maya writes two short lists in her notebook the morning after
beats.summary: After the performance she reviews what went well and what to improve.

beats.scene: Maya studies a hard new task on her office screen
beats.summary: At work Maya is given a new task that she has never done before.

beats.scene: Maya looks at a screen full of buttons while a small voice speaks

beats.scene: A sheet of paper with a large task divided into five small boxes
beats.summary: Maya breaks the big task into small steps, just as she did with the guitar.

beats.scene: Maya clicks through a practice copy of the program with a coffee beside her
beats.summary: Maya practises on a safe copy where mistakes are cheap.

beats.scene: Dev leans over Maya's desk and points kindly at a number on the screen
beats.summary: Maya asks Dev for feedback on her first attempt.

beats.scene: A phone timer shows twenty-five minutes beside a closed notebook

beats.scene: Maya stares at a screen on day ten with her chin on her hand

beats.scene: Maya talks to Colm across a desk, with a calendar between them

B1B2: Maya climbs the steps to her flat with a battered second-hand guitar in her arms. She has just bought it, and she is already telling herself that she is not musical.
Two weeks earlier, a street musician had been playing outside the station on her way home from work. Maya forgot her train, stood still for ten minutes, and felt a wish she had not felt for years.
The next Saturday she walked into a second-hand shop and saw an old guitar hanging on the wall. It had a scratch on its side and cost forty pounds, and she bought it before she could change her mind.
That evening she sits on her bed and stares at the six strings. A small voice tells her that she is not musical, and that the guitar was a waste of money.

Maya knows exactly where that small voice came from, and it is a clear memory. When she was ten, a music teacher asked her to mouth the words in the school choir so that she would not spoil the sound.
After that day, Maya never sang in front of anyone again. She stayed silent at birthday parties, skipped every karaoke night, and decided that music was something that happened to other people.
Maya takes a notepad and writes down the sentence she has believed for so long. Looking at it on paper, she wonders how a sentence can be a fact when nobody has ever tested it.
She finds a free tuning app and spends an hour turning the pegs one by one. By the end, every string rings clearly, and she feels a small, surprising thrill.
The next morning, on the noticeboard of the bakery near her flat, she finds a handwritten card. It says, Guitar lessons for adults, all levels welcome, and signed underneath is the name Ines.
That night Maya sends a short message to the number on the card, and Ines replies within minutes. The first lesson is on Thursday, and Maya decides to treat it as an experiment rather than a test.
On Thursday evening Maya walks to Alder's Bakery with the guitar on her back. Twice she slows down and thinks about turning round, but she keeps walking.
A narrow staircase runs up beside the bakery door, and the smell of warm bread follows her all the way. At the top she finds a small room with a window, two chairs and a music stand.
Ines is a woman in her sixties with silver hair and a green cardigan, and she asks why Maya has come. Maya tells her about the busker and then admits that she is not musical.
Before they play anything, Ines shows Maya how to sit. She checks her back, lowers her shoulders, and rests the guitar so that her arm feels loose and comfortable.
Ines shows her a simple chord, and Maya presses down as hard as she can. The sound that comes out is a dull thud, and the strings dig painfully into her fingertips.
Ines explains that sore fingertips are normal for a beginner. In a few weeks the skin will grow harder where the strings press, and the pain will fade.
When Maya apologises for the noise, Ines smiles and says that everybody sounds terrible at the beginning. She tells Maya that she herself sounded like a cat on a fence for months.
Ines hands her a page of beginner exercises that looks as if it has been used for years. It is covered in pencil marks left by earlier students, and Ines says that every mark is a small struggle.
Instead of telling Maya to learn the song, Ines writes three small tasks on a card. The first is to press one string cleanly, and the others are just as modest.
As she walks home past the closing bakery, Maya realises that she has been bad at something for an hour and survived. Being bad at the start, she thinks, is not the same as being unable.
Back at home, Maya borrows a library book about the brain. It says that people once believed the adult brain was fixed, like a house whose building work was finished.
Later research has shown that this picture was wrong. The brain keeps reshaping itself throughout life, although it changes most easily when we are young.
The book explains that the brain is made of many billions of cells. Each one is linked to thousands of others, and these links are where learning seems to happen.

Think of a faint path across a meadow, the book says, which becomes clearer each time somebody walks along it. Connections in the brain work in a similar way, so repeated practice makes a skill feel easier.

The book describes studies of London taxi drivers, who spend years learning the city's streets. A part of their brains used for memory and finding the way was, on average, larger than in other people.
Another study followed adults who learned to juggle over some weeks. Scans showed small changes in parts of their brains, although scientists still argue about exactly what those changes mean.
The book adds a warning: it is not enough to repeat something without thinking. Careful, focused practice, in which you notice what you are doing, seems to matter most.
That evening Maya presses a single string exactly where Ines showed her, and the note rings out clean and bright. It is only one note, but she plays it three times to be sure.
Maya tells her older brother Theo about the lessons over a cup of tea. He says that some people have a head start, like children whose parents played music at home.
In her notebook, Maya draws a green meadow with a thin line running across it. She decides that every day of practice will be one more walk along that path.
At home Maya practises the first chord from her lesson. One string buzzes every time, however many times she tries it.
The old voice returns, and it sounds very pleased with itself. Maya puts the guitar on the bed and goes to wash the dishes, telling herself that she should have known.
When the dishes are done, she comes back and looks closely at her left hand. The buzz comes from one finger that is lying flat and touching the next string.
She curves the finger so that only its tip touches the string, and she moves it closer to the metal bar. The buzz disappears, and she plays the chord six times in a row.
Maya realises that the buzz was information, a signal about what to change. If she had treated it as a sign of failure, she would never have looked closely enough to find the cause.
On Saturday Theo is coming to visit, and Maya hides the guitar in her bedroom. Standing at the half-open door, she realises that she is afraid of looking foolish.
Maya thinks about how everyone looks foolish at the start of anything new. The fear of looking foolish, she decides, costs far more than the looking foolish itself.
Maya takes a breath, opens the bedroom door and carries the guitar into the living room. It is leaning against the sofa when the doorbell rings.
At the next lesson Maya mentions the buzz, and Ines looks pleased. She says that she would rather hear a student's worst bar than her best one.
Maya starts a list in her notebook with three columns: what happened, why it happened, and how to fix it. The first line is the buzz, and it already has a fix beside it.
Maya plays a few notes for Theo, who claps loudly and smiles. He tells her that she is a natural, and that she must be gifted.
The compliment makes Maya feel wonderful for about ten minutes. Then she starts to worry, because if she is gifted, every mistake from now on will seem like proof that she is not.
At the next lesson Ines notices the pencil marks that Maya has added to the page. She does not say that Maya is gifted, but that the careful way she practised the hard bar really paid off.
Maya reads that in some studies, children praised for being clever chose easier puzzles afterwards. Children praised for their effort were more willing to try harder ones.
Maya begins to see two quite different ways of thinking about ability. In one it is fixed, like height, and in the other it is something that can grow with the right kind of effort.
In her notebook Maya writes two dates, four weeks apart, with a short line beside each. The first says that she could press one string, and the second says that she can change between two chords.
One evening Maya watches a video of a famous guitarist whose fingers fly across the strings. Her own two chords suddenly seem silly, and she feels very small.
Later she remembers that the guitarist's skill is like an iceberg, with only the tip showing above the water. Beneath it lie thousands of hours of practice in rooms where nobody was watching.
Maya decides to compare herself with her own past instead. She props her phone on a pile of books, records thirty seconds of her playing, and calls the file Day 31.
She listens to the recording and winces at every wobble, then laughs at herself. She decides to keep it, and to listen again in a year.
At a lesson, Ines stretches a rubber band between her hands. If it is slack, nothing happens, she says, and if she pulls too far, it snaps.
Ines never gives Maya a piece that is too easy or too hard. Each new piece is chosen so that it sits just beyond what Maya can already play.
The new page is hard, and Maya feels the familiar urge to stop. Ines tells her that feeling something is hard does not mean she is failing, because the feeling is often a sign that she is learning.
With a stopwatch, Maya counts how many times she can change between two chords in one minute. In the first week the answer is nine, and by the fourth week it is twenty-one.
By the fifth week Maya feels as if she has stopped improving. She plays every day, yet nothing seems to change.
For three days Maya leaves the guitar in its case in the corner. Each evening she tells herself she will play tomorrow, and each evening she does not.

Ines tells her that learning is like a staircase with long flat landings between the steps. A flat stretch does not mean that nothing is happening, because the brain is often sorting things out quietly.
Ines adds that a flat stretch sometimes has another cause. If the practice has become comfortable, the brain has no reason to change, so it may be time to raise the challenge a little.
Maya opens the case and goes back to her notebook. Beside the flat days she writes the word landing, and she decides that she will keep walking across them.

Nothing special happens, but on a Tuesday evening in the seventh week the hard chord change suddenly works. Maya plays it three times and then stares at her fingers as if they belonged to someone else.
Maya replaces her vague wish to get good at guitar with two small goals on a card. One is to change between two chords ten times without a buzz, and the other is to play the first line of a song.
After two weeks Maya ticks off the first goal with a green pen. It feels good to be able to say for certain that she did it.
Ines puts a metronome on the shelf and sets it to a slow speed. She asks Maya to play the hard bar so slowly that she cannot possibly make a mistake.
Maya plays the bar slowly, then a tiny bit faster each day. Ines says that if you practise a mistake quickly, you only teach your hands to make it quickly.
Maya decides to play for twenty minutes every evening after work. It sounds too small to matter, but she finds that she can always manage twenty minutes, even on bad days.
Maya learns that twenty minutes every day works better than two hours on Sunday. Research on memory suggests that spreading practice over several days helps people remember more.

One morning Maya wakes up and finds that a chord she struggled with last night now feels easier. Studies suggest that sleep helps the brain store new skills, although how it does so is still being worked out.
Ines tells Maya to turn the music face down and try to play the tune from memory. It feels much harder than reading it, but research suggests that testing yourself helps you remember.
Maya notices that rereading the music feels comfortable and makes her think she knows it. Trying to recall it from memory is harder, but it shows her what she does not yet know.
Maya writes a short routine on a card and tapes it to the music stand. It begins with a slow warm-up, then the hardest bar, a test from memory, and finally a song she loves.
Maya visits Theo and finds him with a Portuguese grammar book and a mug of coffee. He is forty, and he wants to speak to Ana's mother, who was born in Portugal and speaks little English.
Theo admits that he makes mistakes all the time. Last week he said good night to Ana's mother in the middle of the afternoon, and she laughed kindly and corrected him.
Maya and Theo compare notebooks across the table and are surprised by how alike they are. Both have lists of mistakes and fixes, and both have tiny dates in the margins.
Theo has been reading about how adults learn, and he has some good news. Children often pick up sounds more easily, but adults have strengths too, such as focus, experience and knowing what works.
On the stairs above the bakery, Maya meets Walter, who is seventy-three. He began learning the guitar two years ago and is waiting for his lesson after hers.
Walter plays a slow tune for her, and it is not perfect. It is warm and steady, and Maya understands that he is proud of it, and with good reason.
In her notebook Maya crosses out the words I can't play this and writes I can't play this yet. She notices that the second sentence makes her ask what to try next.
Maya thinks about how many things she gave up on without really trying. Walter and Theo have taught her that being busy or being older is often an excuse and not a rule.
Theo explains his secret, which is to talk to himself in Portuguese while he cooks. He makes mistakes, but he is using the language, and that matters more than being correct.

That evening Ana's mother speaks slowly to Theo, and he understands a whole sentence. His face lights up, and Maya realises that she is looking at a grown man who has just proved something to himself.
While Maya plays, Ines leans over her shoulder and points at her left hand. Maya had no idea that her thumb was sticking up above the neck of the guitar.
Ines explains why we so often miss our own mistakes when we practise. We feel what we meant to do, so it is hard to notice what we actually did.
Maya props her phone on a pile of books and films her hands for one minute. When she watches the video, she sees the thumb, and a second habit she never knew about.
Maya notices that Ines gives only one piece of feedback at a time. It is specific, it comes right away, and it tells Maya what to try next, not just what was wrong.
Ines writes some notes about Maya's playing, with three things to improve. Maya reads them calmly, because she has learned to treat criticism as being about the work, and not about her worth.

Even so, the notes sting a little, and Maya's first instinct is to defend herself. She goes for a walk around the block, and when she returns she finds that the notes are fairer than they first seemed.
Walter overhears Maya playing as he waits on the stairs, and he says that her left shoulder is creeping up towards her ear. He is not an expert, but he has noticed something real.

Not all advice is helpful, as Maya learns when a stranger at a pub tells her that guitars are too hard. She decides to ask three questions about any advice: does this person know, how do they know, and is it about my playing?
Maya realises that she needs both kinds of people. Theo's praise keeps her cheerful and Ines's corrections keep her improving, and neither would be enough without the other.
Maya sticks a note on her guitar with the single word thumb. Fixing the habit is hard because the new position feels wrong, even though it is right.
Maya's friend Joss is having a party in the spring, and he has heard about the lessons. He asks her to play something, and before she has time to think, she says yes.
At the party Maya sits in the middle of a crowded living room and starts a song she knows well. She stops twice, apologises too often, and feels her face grow hot.
Afterwards the party carries on as if nothing has happened, with friends laughing and talking in the bright room. Maya sits in a corner with a glass of water, sure that everybody has seen her fail.
Walking home in the rain, Maya replays every mistake like a film she cannot turn off. By the time she reaches her door, she has decided that she is not a musician after all.
On Thursday Maya tells Ines about the party and calls it a disaster. Ines pours some tea and asks her to describe the faces she saw in the room.

The next day Maya asks Joss what he thought of her song, braced for polite pity. He says that it was nice and that he was mostly worried about the pizza, and he truly seems to have forgotten the rest.
Maya reads that psychologists have found people tend to overestimate how closely others observe them. This habit of mind is sometimes called the spotlight effect, and it is very common.
Maya makes a list of what really went wrong, and it is a short one. She had only ever played alone, and she had never rehearsed with people in the room.
Ines tells Maya about her first concert, when she forgot the second verse and started the first one again. She says that Maya should speak to herself as kindly as she would speak to a friend.
On Friday evening Maya takes the guitar out of its case and plays for three minutes, with nobody listening. The party was one bad evening, she tells herself, and not a final judgement.

Maya's old friend Priya started the guitar around the same time, and she comes round with her own instrument. She plays a quick, lively tune without a single mistake, and Maya watches her fingers closely.
After Priya has gone home, Maya sits in the kitchen and admits that she felt envy. She is ashamed of it, because Priya is her friend and has done nothing wrong.
Maya remembers that even an uncomfortable feeling can carry useful information about her. Her envy shows her exactly what she wants, so she decides to ask Priya how she practises.
Priya laughs and explains that she played the violin from the age of eight. She already reads music and knows how to practise, and much of that knowledge carries over to the guitar.
Priya also admits that she practises forty minutes every day, usually on her lunch break in the park. There is no secret, she says, and her speed has a plain cause.
Maya accepts that people do learn at different speeds, and that some things come faster to some people than to others. But learning is not a race, and nobody gives out prizes for finishing first.
Priya offers to teach Maya how to read a chord chart. In return, Maya shows her friend the notebook with the mistakes list, which Priya thinks is a brilliant idea.
Maya notices that Priya rushes ahead of the beat and has never practised slowly. She lends her the metronome, and Priya is surprised by how hard it is to play slowly.
Maya decides that other people can be used in two ways. A ruler measures you and makes you feel small, but a map shows you where it is possible to go.
At the end of the evening the two friends try a duet on two simple chords. It is messy and out of time, but they laugh until they cannot play.
Theo brings his seven-year-old daughter Nell to visit, and she begs to try the guitar. Maya carefully places Nell's small fingers on the strings and shows her a simple chord.
Nell asks why the sound is so thin when she presses the strings softly, and Maya has no idea. She says that they will find out together, which delights Nell.
Maya discovers that explaining a chord is much harder than playing it. Every time she tries to put it into words, she finds a gap in her own understanding.
Maya begins to explain each new idea out loud to the plant on her windowsill. Studies suggest that explaining something to someone else, or even to yourself, helps people understand and remember it.
One evening Maya plays a minor chord, and it sounds sad. She wonders why, and the next day she asks Ines.
