The sensible response, she suggested, is to stay patient and also to raise the challenge a little.

That evening Maya opened the case at last, picked up her notebook and wrote the word landing beside every flat week. The label changed the feeling of the pages, since a landing is a place on a staircase, not a hole in a floor. She then played for twenty minutes, not brilliantly, but with the quiet stubbornness of someone who has chosen to continue.

Nothing remarkable preceded it, but on a Tuesday evening in the seventh week the difficult chord change simply worked. Maya played it once, then twice, then a third time, and then stared at her fingers as though they had been replaced by somebody else's. The stairs, it seemed, had been climbing quietly while she stood on the landing and doubted them.

Maya replaced her vague wish to become good at the guitar with two small goals, written on a card and pinned above her desk. One was to change between two chords ten times without a buzz, and the other was to play the first line of a favourite song from start to finish. A wish gives you nothing to aim at, whereas a clear target tells you what to do this evening.

After two weeks of work Maya ticked off the first goal with a green pen and felt a small, clean satisfaction. A goal that can be checked has a particular advantage, because it lets you say with certainty that you did it, whereas a vague wish can never be fulfilled or failed. Research on goal setting generally supports the idea, although, as Ines pointed out, the goal must be difficult enough to matter and small enough to reach.

Ines placed a small ticking metronome on the shelf and set it to a speed that seemed almost absurdly slow. She asked Maya to play the hard bar at that pace, so slowly that she could not possibly make a mistake, and to raise the speed only when it felt easy. Maya, who had always assumed that fast was the goal, felt her fingers relax for the first time all week.

Day by day Maya nudged the metronome up by a tiny step, and each time she kept the playing clean before moving on. Ines had explained that if you practise a mistake at speed you simply teach your hands to repeat it at speed, whereas careful repetition builds the right pattern first. Speed, it seemed, is not something you chase; it is something that arrives when accuracy has been patient enough.

Maya settled on twenty minutes every evening, which sounded far too small to matter and turned out to be wonderfully hard to avoid. She could always manage twenty minutes, even after the worst day at work, whereas a promised two hours on Sunday had a way of dissolving into other plans. Short sessions, taken regularly, seemed to suit her busy life and, as it happened, her brain as well.

Maya discovered that twenty minutes every evening served her better than a single heroic session at the weekend. Research on memory has repeatedly suggested that learning spread over many days is held far more securely than learning crammed into a few hours. The brain, it seems, likes to be visited often, in the manner of a garden that is watered a little at a time.

One morning Maya woke to discover that a chord that had defeated her the night before now felt noticeably easier. Studies suggest that sleep helps the brain to store and organise new skills, particularly movements and sequences, although the precise mechanisms are still being worked out. It was a pleasing thought that a part of her practice was being done while she lay in bed doing nothing at all.

Ines told Maya to turn the sheet face down and to try to play the tune from memory, which felt uncomfortably like being caught without homework. Research suggests that the act of pulling something out of memory strengthens it far more than studying it again, even though the effort feels slower and the early results look worse. Struggle, once more, was turning out to be the useful part of the whole business, and not the enemy.

Maya noticed that rereading the music gave her a pleasant sense of familiarity, which she mistook for knowledge. Trying to recall the tune from memory was far more uncomfortable, but it exposed exactly which bars she did not know and sent her back to those. Feeling that you know something and actually knowing it, she concluded, are two quite different conditions.

Maya gathered what she had learned and wrote a short routine on a card, which she taped to the music stand. It began with a slow warm-up and moved on to the hardest bar, a test from memory and a break, before ending with a song she simply loved playing. The routine took twenty minutes, it asked very little of her willpower, and over the following weeks it quietly turned practice from a chore into a habit.

Maya called at Theo's house one Sunday and found him hunched over a Portuguese grammar book with a cooling mug of coffee beside him. At forty he had decided to learn the language so that he could talk properly to his wife Ana's mother, who had been born in Portugal and spoke very little English. His brow was creased with concentration, and he looked exactly as Maya felt at her music stand.

Theo cheerfully admitted that he made mistakes all the time, and he had a fresh example ready. The previous week he had wished Ana's mother good night in the middle of the afternoon, and she had laughed warmly and corrected him with the right words. It was clear that the laughter had not wounded him; he had simply filed the correction away and moved on.

Maya and Theo laid their notebooks side by side on the table and were startled by how alike they looked. Each held lists of mistakes with their causes, each had small dates in the margin, and each recorded the little victories in the same cautious, understated way. It was a pleasant discovery that two such different skills could be learned by the same careful habits.

Theo had been reading about how adults learn, and he summarised it with the relish of a man who had found good news. Children often pick up accents and sounds more easily and are less afraid of mistakes, but adults bring focus, experience, stronger general knowledge and a clearer idea of which methods suit them. Each age has its own advantages, in other words, and age is not a locked door.

On the stairs above the bakery one Thursday, Maya met Walter, a retired bus driver of seventy-three with large, gentle hands. He had started the guitar two years earlier, he told her, after a lifetime of saying that he was too old and too busy, and he was waiting for his own lesson to begin. His fingers moved slowly, but he spoke about each small improvement with the delight of a child who had found a coin.

Walter played her a slow tune on the stairs, and it was not perfect, since the timing wavered and one chord was a little muddy. Yet it was warm and steady and unmistakably music, and the satisfaction on his face was complete. Maya saw that his years had not closed the door on learning; they had only changed the speed.

In her notebook Maya crossed out a sentence that she had been writing for weeks, I can't play this, and replaced it with a longer one, I can't play this yet. The change was small, but she noticed that the first sentence closed the subject while the second opened it and invited her to ask what she might try next. Words are not magic, but the words we use about ourselves do seem to steer what we attempt.

Walking home, Maya counted all the things she had once abandoned without a proper attempt, from swimming to chess to speaking a second language. Walter and Theo had made it harder to blame age, or the lack of time, and she was forced to admit that those were often excuses wearing the clothes of reasons. This is not to say that adult life is easy, because it is not; it is only to say that the door is rarely locked.

Theo revealed his secret in the kitchen, where he narrated the cooking aloud in careful, mistaken Portuguese. Onions, he declared to the empty room, were being cut, and the pot was becoming hot. He was using the language rather than merely studying it, and that, he said, mattered more to him than being right, which was a principle Maya decided to borrow for her guitar.

At dinner that evening Ana's mother spoke slowly to Theo, choosing each word with care, and he understood a whole sentence for the first time. His face lit up like a child's, and the table erupted in warm applause, while Maya watched with her own private happiness. Here was a grown man of forty who had just proved to himself, in front of his family, that he could still learn.

While Maya played, Ines leaned over her shoulder and quietly pointed at her left hand. Maya looked down and saw to her surprise that her thumb was sticking up high above the neck, a habit she had never once noticed in weeks of practice. It is a curious feature of learning that the mistakes we make most often are frequently the ones we cannot see.

Ines explained why the thumb had gone unnoticed for so long, and her explanation was simple and rather humbling. When we practise, we feel the intention behind each movement more strongly than the movement itself, so our minds quietly report what we meant to do and not what we did. Another pair of eyes, or a pair of ears, can often see the gap that we cannot.

Maya propped her phone against a pile of books and filmed her hands for a single minute, then watched the result with the detachment of a stranger. There was the thumb, as Ines had said, and also a second habit she had never suspected, a little jerk of the wrist before every chord change. A camera, she realised, is the most patient and least flattering teacher that money can buy.

Maya began to notice how Ines gave feedback, and the method was almost invisible once she saw it. It was specific rather than vague, it came straight after the playing and not a week later, and it concentrated on a single next step in place of a heap of complaints. Good feedback, she decided, is like a good map, since what matters is not how many roads it shows but which one to take now.

Ines wrote a short page of notes after the lesson, listing three things that needed to improve. A year earlier Maya would have read it as a catalogue of her failings, but she now read it as a description of the work, with no verdict on the worker. Criticism is about what you did, she reminded herself, and it says nothing at all about what you are worth.

Even so, the notes stung, and her first instinct was to argue with them, silently and at length. She took a walk around the block instead, letting the hurt fade a little, and when she read the page again it seemed fair and perfectly kind. A sting is a normal reaction to criticism, and it often helps to wait until it has passed before deciding what the criticism is worth.

Walter, waiting on the stairs for his lesson, overheard Maya playing and tactfully offered one observation: her left shoulder was creeping up towards her ear. He was no expert and said so himself, yet he had noticed something that neither Maya nor Ines had mentioned, because each pair of eyes sees a little differently. It was a useful reminder that feedback can come from unexpected places, provided that you are willing to listen.

Not all feedback is worth keeping, as Maya learned when a confident stranger at a pub informed her that the guitar was far too difficult to learn properly after thirty. She found that three questions helped her to sort the useful from the useless: does this person actually know, how do they know, and are they commenting on my playing or on their own opinions? The stranger, she concluded, had never played a note in his life, and his advice was worth exactly what it had cost her, which was nothing.

Maya realised that she needed two quite different kinds of people in her corner, and that she was lucky to have both. Theo's warm praise kept her cheerful on difficult evenings, while Ines's honest corrections kept her improving, and neither would have been enough alone. Encouragement without truth leaves us comfortable and stuck, and truth without encouragement can leave us discouraged and silent.

Maya stuck a yellow note on the neck of her guitar bearing the single word thumb, and for weeks she glanced at it in every practice. The correct position felt awkward and even wrong at first, while the old, faulty one felt natural, which is a common and slightly confusing feature of changing a habit. Only after several weeks of patient repetition did the new way begin to feel like her own.

In the spring Maya's friend Joss invited her to a party at his house, having heard about the lessons from someone else. He asked whether she would play something for everyone, in the cheerful tone of a man who assumed that the answer would be no. Before the sensible part of her could intervene, she heard herself say yes, and she regretted it almost at once.

At the party she perched on a stool in the middle of the crowded living room and began a song that she had played perfectly at home. Her hands shook, her mind went blank at the second verse, and she stopped twice, apologising so many times that the song became almost an afterthought. When it ended, her face was burning and she wanted to disappear through the floor.

Afterwards the party flowed on as though nothing had happened, with friends laughing and talking in the bright, noisy room. Maya sat in a corner with a glass of water, convinced that every eye had been on her and that every ear had registered each mistake. The old voice, which had been silent for weeks, returned with a note of quiet triumph.

She walked home through the drizzle, replaying each mistake like a film that she could not switch off. By the time she reached her door she had reached a verdict as well, which was that she was not a musician and never had been, and that the past three months had been a pleasant mistake. She did not touch the guitar for two days, and the case stayed shut in the corner.

On Thursday Maya confessed what had happened, using the word disaster several times in the first minute. Ines poured two cups of tea and, instead of offering comfort, asked her to describe the faces that she had seen in the room while she was playing. Maya opened her mouth and discovered, to her annoyance, that she could not remember a single one.

The next day Maya braced herself and asked Joss what he had thought of her performance, expecting some form of polite pity. He looked puzzled, said that it had been very nice, and admitted that he had been mostly worried about whether the pizza had arrived. He remembered almost nothing of the song, and certainly nothing of the mistakes, which had loomed so large in her own memory.

Maya looked into the matter and found that psychologists have repeatedly observed a habit of mind sometimes called the spotlight effect. People tend to overestimate how closely others watch them, and how long the others remember their slips, because each of us lives at the centre of our own story. We feel as though a bright lamp is shining on every mistake, when most people are busy worrying about their own.

Maya made a list of what had really gone wrong, and she was surprised by how short and practical it was. She had only ever played alone, she had never rehearsed with anyone listening, and she had agreed to perform on an impulse and not as a plan. None of these causes had anything to do with talent, and each of them could be mended.

Ines then told the story of her own first concert, at which she had forgotten the second verse and calmly begun the first again, hoping that nobody would notice. Somebody had, but the world carried on, and she had learned something from it. She urged Maya to speak to herself as kindly as she would to a friend, and added that studies suggest self-kindness helps people try again after a failure.

On Friday evening she lifted the guitar out of its case and played for three quiet minutes, with nobody listening and nothing to prove. The party, she decided, had been one bad evening and not a final judgement, and what it had really revealed was how much she still had to practise in front of other people. She felt the old path across the meadow begin to open again under her feet.

Maya's old friend Priya, who had taken up the guitar at about the same time, came round one evening with her own instrument and a mischievous smile. She played a quick, lively tune without a single hesitation, her fingers skipping across the strings, while Maya watched in a silence that was only partly admiration. Underneath the applause, something small and sharp had begun to prick at her, and she did not like the feeling.

After Priya had gone, Maya sat in the kitchen with a cold mug of tea and admitted what she had felt. It was envy, plain and unflattering, and she was ashamed of it, since Priya was a good friend who had done nothing to deserve it. She tried at first to push the feeling away, but it stayed in the room like an uninvited guest.

Then Maya remembered that feelings, even uncomfortable ones, can carry information, and she looked at her envy again with some curiosity. It was telling her very precisely what she wanted, which was to play fluently and easily, and that was something she could work towards. Instead of resenting Priya for being good, she would simply ask her how she had done it.

Priya laughed, then explained that she had played the violin from the age of eight and had only recently given it up. She already read music, had a trained ear and understood, in her bones, how to practise, and a good deal of that knowledge had carried over to the guitar. Skills often transfer from one field to another, which is one reason why two people who start on the same day are rarely on the same footing.

Priya also confessed, a little sheepishly, that she practised forty minutes every single day, usually on a park bench at lunchtime. There was no secret, and no special gift involved, but a plain accumulation of hours, which was twice what Maya had been doing. The speed that had looked like magic turned out to have an ordinary and entirely visible cause.

Maya accepted, with an honest effort, that people really do learn at different speeds, and that some skills come more easily to some than to others. The difference, however, mattered much less than she had feared, because learning is not a race with a single finishing line, and nobody hands out medals for getting there first. What counted was whether she was moving forward, not whether she was moving at Priya's pace.

Priya offered to teach Maya how to read a chord chart, a skill that would save her hours of confusion. In return Maya showed her friend the notebook with its three-column list of mistakes, and Priya, who had never kept such a thing, declared it a brilliant idea and begged to borrow the format. The two of them realised that they could be useful to each other, and the sting of envy melted into something much warmer.

Maya noticed something that she would never have seen while she was busy being envious: Priya rushed ahead of the beat, and her timing wobbled whenever the tune became complicated. She lent her friend the metronome, and Priya was startled to discover how difficult it was to play slowly and accurately. Nobody, it appeared, was simply the talented one, since each of them had strengths and weak spots of her own.

Maya resolved that other people, when they are better than we are, can serve us in two quite different capacities. If you use them as a ruler, they measure you and make you feel small, but if you use them as a map, they show you where it is possible to go and how others have got there. From then on, whenever she watched someone play better than she did, she asked herself what she could learn from the route.

At the end of the evening the two friends tried a duet, built on two simple chords and a good deal of optimism. It was messy, wildly out of time and quite impossible to take seriously, and they laughed until neither could play another note. For a few minutes Maya forgot all about progress and remembered that she had picked up a guitar for the pleasure of making music.

Theo brought his seven-year-old daughter Nell to visit one Saturday, and Nell, who had been eyeing the guitar for some time, begged to try it. Maya knelt beside her and gently placed the small fingers on the strings, explaining the chord shape as clearly as she could. It was the first time that she had ever taught anybody anything on the instrument, and it felt oddly grand.

Nell asked why the sound was so thin when she pressed softly, why the thick strings were so low and why the guitar had a hole in it. Maya realised, with a small jolt, that she had no idea about half of the answers, and she had been playing for months. She told Nell that they would find out together, which pleased the child enormously.

Maya discovered that explaining a chord was a good deal harder than playing it, and the difficulty taught her something at once. Every time she tried to put the shape into words, she stumbled upon a gap, a place where her fingers knew what to do but her mind could not say why. Teaching, she realised, is a kind of examination in which the examiner is yourself.

Feeling a little foolish, Maya began explaining each new idea aloud to the plant on her windowsill, as though it were an unusually quiet pupil. Studies suggest that teaching, or even preparing to teach, tends to help people understand and remember material better than simply studying it. The plant, as far as she could tell, learned nothing, but Maya learned a great deal.

One evening Maya played a minor chord and tilted her head, struck by how plainly sad it sounded. She wondered what exactly made it so, and the next day she asked Ines, who was pleased to be asked. Curiosity about why things work, she was finding, made the learning stick far better than any amount of obedient repetition.

Ines explained that a minor chord differs from its major cousin by a single note, which is lowered by one small step. Many listeners hear that tiny change as sadder or darker, although part of the effect is probably learned from the music of the culture that we grow up in. A whole mood, Maya marvelled, could hang on the movement of a single finger across one string.

Maya also discovered the answer to Nell's question about the strings, which was beautifully simple. A thicker, longer or looser string vibrates more slowly, and a slower vibration gives a lower note, while a thin, tight string rattles quickly and sounds high. Knowing the reason made the instrument seem less like a mystery box and more like a machine that she was beginning to understand.

Maya began a page in her notebook headed Why, and she filled it with questions as they occurred to her, sometimes a dozen in one evening. Research suggests that when people are curious about a question, they tend to remember its answer better, and the answers she found certainly stayed with her. The page became a collection of small mysteries, each one solved and each one a little more satisfying than the last.

Nell's fingers were far too small to reach the chord, and the sound was a cheerful rattle that made the plant tremble. She laughed, announced that it was terrible and demanded to try again, without a flicker of embarrassment. Young children, Maya observed, have not yet learned to be ashamed of being bad at things, and that is perhaps their greatest advantage.

Nell looked up with a serious face and asked Maya outright whether she was good at the guitar. Maya thought about it for a moment and answered that she was not good yet, but that she was getting better every week. Nell nodded as if this were a perfectly complete and sensible reply, and returned to the strings.

Maya decided that she wanted to learn a whole song and not merely a string of exercises. She chose a slow folk song called The Water Is Wide, which she had loved since childhood and had hummed in the bath for years without ever imagining that she could play it. It was a little beyond her, in the way that Ines liked, and she hoped that it would be worth the reach.

Maya arranged her desk so that a video, a chord book and the guitar were all within reach, and she moved between them as the mood took her. The video showed her how the hands moved, the book showed her the pattern behind the chords, and the guitar told her at once whether she had understood. Each way of learning, she found, revealed something that the others had left out.

Maya came across the popular claim that each person has a single learning style, such as visual or auditory, and she was surprised to learn that it has little support in the research. What does appear to help, according to the studies, is meeting an idea in several forms, so that you see it, hear it, say it and do it. Her cluttered desk, it turned out, was a perfectly reasonable laboratory after all, though she did not tidy it.

Maya hummed the tune and tried to find its notes on the guitar without any written music, a method that she had always supposed to be reserved for the talented. She made dozens of wrong guesses, but each one narrowed the search, since a wrong note tells you what the right one is not. When the melody finally emerged, she felt that she had been a detective rather than a performer.

Priya's lesson on reading a chord chart now paid off handsomely, for the page showed Maya the order of the chords and exactly where each one began. Instead of fumbling from one chord to the next, she could see the entire shape of the song at a glance, with its repeated patterns and its familiar turns. It was a map, she thought, and maps are best studied before the journey begins.

For a whole week Maya remained stuck on a single bar in the middle of the song, playing it again and again with the same stubborn failure. At last she decided to keep the goal and change the method, and she began experimenting with different speeds, fingerings and even different positions of the hand. When a path is blocked, it is wiser to look for another route than to push harder against the same wall.

One of her experiments was to learn the last bar of the difficult section first, and then the one before it, and so on, working backwards through the passage. Every run therefore ended on a part that she knew well, and her confidence grew as the familiar stretch lengthened. The bar that had defeated her for a week gave way in two evenings.

Maya studied her practice notes and noticed an uncomfortable fact: on several evenings she had spent twenty minutes repeating the same mistake, and so she had practised the mistake rather than the music. Effort, she concluded, is necessary but not sufficient, and it must be steered by a sound strategy and by feedback that tells you whether you are travelling in the right direction. Working hard on the wrong thing is merely a tiring way to stand still.

Ines suggested that Maya mix her practice and not drill one chord for twenty minutes before moving to the next. Studies suggest that shuffling several skills within a session feels clumsier and slower at the time, yet often leaves people better able to use them later, because the brain must keep choosing what to do. Maya tried it, felt irritated at the confusion, and was pleasantly surprised a week later.

One evening in the middle of the autumn, Maya played The Water Is Wide from the first note to the last without stopping. It wobbled in two places and lurched in a third, but the melody was unmistakable and complete, and she felt her eyes grow bright. Months earlier she had been unable to press a single string without a buzz.

After a punishing week at work, Maya sat down to practise and discovered that nothing whatever would go in. Her fingers fumbled, her attention slid away and the chords that she knew perfectly well seemed to belong to somebody else. She put the guitar on a chair and sank under a blanket on the sofa, too tired even to feel guilty.

She had been sleeping badly for several nights, and in the morning she saw the connection between that and her useless evening. Research on sleep is fairly clear on this point, for a tired brain finds it harder to pay attention, to hold new information and to store what it has learned. Learning, she realised, does not happen in a mind that is running on empty.

Maya made a decision that would once have felt like laziness, and she skipped her practice for a single evening in order to go to bed early. The following day the chords flowed more easily than they had for a week, as though her fingers had been oiled in the night. Rest, she saw, was not the opposite of work but a necessary part of it, like the pause between two notes.

Ines advised her to take a short break whenever her attention began to flag, and certainly after about twenty minutes. Attention is not unlimited, she said, and some studies suggest that a few minutes of quiet rest, without a screen, may even help the brain to hold on to what it has just learned. Maya began to make a cup of tea in the middle of every session and found that she was sharper afterwards.

Maya began to walk along the river path at sunrise before work, partly from curiosity and partly because she had run out of better ideas. She soon noticed that her mood was brighter and her mind clearer, which fitted with studies suggesting that regular exercise can help attention and memory, although the effects are modest. It was not a miracle cure, but it cost nothing and she enjoyed the herons.

Maya read widely about food and the brain, and she found a good deal of nonsense mixed in with the sense. No special food, it seems, will turn a person into a genius, and the real advice was plain and rather dull, namely regular meals, enough water, daylight and enough sleep. She was relieved to find that she did not have to buy anything at all, least of all a miracle.

Ines explained that when people feel too much pressure, their thinking can narrow and their attention can fix on the fear and not on the task. This is sometimes called choking, and it afflicts skilled performers as well as beginners, which Maya found oddly comforting. Calm, by contrast, leaves the mind free to use everything that it has practised.

Ines taught her a simple trick, which was to take three slow breaths before attempting a difficult passage, breathing out for longer than she breathed in. Slow breathing can help to calm the body, and a calmer body, as a general rule, plays with more control. It sounded too modest to matter, but Maya tried it every day for a week and began to rely on it.

To test the idea, Maya played the same hard bar twice, once with her shoulders hunched around her ears and once after three slow breaths and a deliberate sigh. The difference was not subtle, since the second attempt was smoother, steadier and far less frightening. It was a small experiment, but she liked results that she could hear for herself.

Maya planned her weeks with new care, so that they included regular practice, early walks, proper sleep and one full day in which she did not touch the guitar. She was surprised to find that she improved faster with the rest day than she had without it, as though the pause gave her progress somewhere to settle. Learning, she decided, is a rhythm of effort and recovery and never merely a heap of effort.

At the end of a lesson in November, Ines mentioned that she held a small winter evening each December for her students and their friends. She asked, in the most casual way, whether Maya would like to play one piece there, four weeks from now. Maya felt the room tilt slightly, as though the floor had suddenly become a stage.

Maya remembered the party at Joss's house, the stool and the burning in her face, and for a long moment she said nothing at all. Ines did not hurry her or push her, but simply waited, with the patience of a woman who had watched many students arrive at the same cliff edge. The silence stretched until Maya heard herself ask what would be different this time.

Ines counted the differences on her fingers: this time there would be a plan, a small and friendly audience of people who wished her well, and four weeks of deliberate preparation. The party had been an accident, whereas this would be a project, and a project can be rehearsed. Maya felt her fear shift a little, from a fog into something with edges that she could measure.

Maya took a deep breath, felt her pulse leap and said yes, before the fear could organise a rebuttal. She resolved to treat the evening as another experiment, one that would show her what she could do when she prepared properly and was not taken by surprise. Whatever happened, she told herself, she would learn something, and that was a comforting thought to hold on to.

At home Maya wrote the date on her calendar and circled it in a firm blue ring, and the circle seemed to hum with a faint menace. Then she worked backwards from it, deciding what she would need to have achieved by the end of each week, so that the last week would be for polishing and not for panic. A plan does not remove the fear, but it gives the fear somewhere useful to go.

Maya chose The Water Is Wide, the song that she could now play successfully about eight times in every ten, which Ines considered about right for a performance. She marked the three hardest bars with a pencil and decided to attack them first, in each session, while her mind was fresh and her fingers willing. The easy parts, she knew, would look after themselves, and she could polish them in the final week.

She prepared with deliberate care, attacking the hardest bars first, while her mind was fresh and her fingers willing. Only at the end of each evening did she play the entire song without stopping, as though performing for an invisible audience. By the third week the difficult passages had stopped feeling like walls and begun to feel like ordinary hills.

Ines then gave her an unusual exercise: she was to make a mistake on purpose, in the middle of the song, and carry on as though nothing had happened. Maya felt ridiculous at first, but she practised it until a wrong note no longer made her heart jump, since recovery is a skill like any other. If you have rehearsed the stumble, she realised, then the stumble loses most of its power over you.

Maya played the song first for her houseplant, then for Walter on the stairs, then for Theo and Nell, and finally for four friends crowded into her small living room. Each audience was slightly larger than the last, and each time her hands shook a little less, as though she were climbing a ladder rung by rung. Gradual exposure, as she had read, is a gentle way to teach the body that an audience is not a danger.

Walter confided, in the stairwell before a lesson, that even at seventy-three his hands shook before he played in front of anyone. Nerves, he said, were simply a sign that something mattered, and he would have been sad to lose the feeling, since it meant that he still cared. Some researchers suggest that calling the feeling excitement, instead of fear, can help a little, since the body feels much the same either way.

On the day before the evening Maya packed a bag with a spare string, a tuner and a bottle of water, following the checklist that Ines had given her. She played the song once, resisted every temptation to cram, and went to bed early, trusting that her sleep would do part of the work. It is strange how hard it can be to stop practising when the thing that you most need is rest.

On the evening itself, the small room above the bakery glowed with candles on every windowsill and every shelf. About fifteen people sat on mismatched chairs, among them Theo, Ana, Nell and Priya, while the warm smell of bread drifted up the stairs. It looked less like a stage than like a family sitting room, and Maya's shoulders dropped a fraction.

Walter played first, and his hands trembled just as he had warned, but the tune was warm and steady. He slipped once on a chord, paused for half a breath and went on, and the audience applauded him as though he had played in a great hall. Maya saw, with great relief, that nobody in the room was sitting there waiting for perfection.

When Ines called her name, Maya's hands turned cold and her heart began a heavy drumming. She took the three slow breaths that she had rehearsed, felt her shoulders loosen a little and sat down in the circle of candlelight with the guitar on her knee. Every face in the room was turned towards her, and every one of them was kind.

The opening notes of The Water Is Wide rang out clear and sweet in the hush of the room. Her hands settled, her breathing steadied and for several bars the music seemed to flow of its own accord, as it had so often in her own living room. She had not known that she could feel so calm in front of people.

Halfway through the song Maya's third finger slipped, and a wrong note rang out into the silence like a dropped plate. Her heart leapt, the familiar heat rose in her face and for one dreadful moment the old voice began to speak. Then she remembered the exercise that she had practised so many times, and the moment became a choice.

This time she neither stopped nor apologised but took a breath and carried on, exactly as she had rehearsed on dozens of evenings. The music closed over the wrong note like water over a stone, and the next chord arrived in its proper place. It felt like crossing a river on slippery stones and finding, to her amazement, that she had not fallen.

Maya played the final chord and let it ring until it faded into the candlelight. The room was silent for a heartbeat, and then it filled with warm applause, while Nell, who had been told to be quiet, let out a loud and joyful cheer. Maya sat with her hands trembling, her face flushed and a smile spreading across it that she could not have stopped if she had tried.

Afterwards a woman in a green scarf told Maya how much she had loved the second verse, and not one person mentioned the wrong note. That night Maya lay awake for hours, her body humming with leftover energy, which Ines had warned her was entirely natural after such an effort. It is hard to switch off a nervous system that has just been through something important.

The next morning, over coffee, Maya wrote two short lists in her notebook: what had gone well, and what she would like to improve. She tried to look back as a kind coach might, honest about the faults but without a trace of blame. Reflection of this sort turns an experience into a lesson, and a lesson into a better next attempt.

In the first week of January, Maya's manager Colm, a brisk man who disliked long explanations, handed her a task that she had never attempted. She was to learn a new program for planning delivery routes and to produce a first report within two weeks. The screen looked like the cockpit of an aeroplane, and she felt her old dread stir.

A familiar voice informed her that she had never been technical, that others would learn it faster and that she would be found out. This time she recognised it at once, as the same old story wearing a different coat, and she remembered how little evidence it had ever possessed. Knowing that the voice was a habit, and not a fact, took away much of its force.

Maya did what she had done with the guitar and divided the daunting task into five smaller ones on a sheet of paper. The first step was merely to plan one very simple route from beginning to end, and she decided to think of nothing beyond it for the rest of the day. By lunchtime she had done it, and the cockpit looked a little less alarming.

Dev, a calm and generous colleague, showed Maya a practice copy of the program in which nothing was real and nothing could go wrong. She could make as many mistakes as she liked there without disturbing a single customer, and she made a great many, very quickly. Practising where the cost of a mistake is small is one of the cleverest ways to learn anything.

Maya showed Dev her first attempt and asked him, in a voice only slightly shaky, what he saw. He pointed out two things that she could not have noticed on her own, a wrong setting and a missing check, and he said both kindly and without fuss. Asking for feedback, she thought, had become the quickest shortcut to improvement that she knew, and also the kindest.

Maya studied the program for twenty-five minutes each morning, then closed her notes and tried to carry out the task from memory. It felt slower and less comfortable than simply rereading the instructions, yet she remembered far more of it, exactly as the research had promised. She had borrowed the whole method from the guitar, and it seemed to work in an office just as well.

On the tenth day Maya felt that she had stopped improving, and the familiar dismay began to rise in her chest. Then, quite unexpectedly, she smiled, because she recognised the landing on the staircase and remembered that the next step usually came when she had stopped looking for it. She kept her twenty-five minutes, trusted the process and went home on time, feeling oddly light.

Colm had hoped that she would master the program in a week, so Maya explained, with the plan open in front of her, that she would need about three. She showed him the five steps and the way she was testing herself, and he listened, frowned and finally agreed to the longer timetable. Being honest about how long learning takes, she discovered, is often respected and rarely punished.

At the end of the third week Maya sent in her first report, and it was correct and on time. The habits that she had built for the guitar, breaking big jobs into steps, welcoming feedback and tolerating the awkward early days, had come with her into the office without being asked. The habits of learning, she found, are not tied to a single subject but travel with you.

That evening Maya wrote a short list headed Things I know about learning, and she was startled to see how long it had become. It included practising slowly, testing herself, welcoming feedback, resting properly and treating a mistake as a clue, and she had not known any of it a year before. Learning how to learn, she realised, is itself a skill that can be improved, and the improvement carries over into everything else.

On a Saturday afternoon at Theo's house, Maya sat watching Nell wrestle with a large jigsaw puzzle of a harbour. Pieces that ought to have fitted refused to, her small face was growing red, and the corner of her mouth had begun to tremble. It was a scene that Maya recognised from the inside, having lived through so many like it.

Maya felt a powerful urge to lean over and slot the piece into place, and to spare the child the discomfort of not knowing. She kept her hands firmly in her lap, since solving the problem for Nell would also steal from her the learning that lay in the struggle. Some difficulty, studies of children suggest, is productive, provided that it is not so great that it leads to despair.

Nell flung a piece onto the table, folded her arms and announced that she was stupid and could never do it. Maya heard her own old voice coming out of a seven-year-old, and the sound made her heart ache, because children pick up such sentences so early. She understood that whatever she said next might matter a great deal, and she chose her words with care.

Maya resisted the temptation to say that Nell was clever or that she was certainly not stupid, since both answers would put the subject on talent. Instead she pointed to the finished corner and said that Nell had tried the corners first, which was a very good plan, and that she had not given up. Praise that names what a child did gives her something that she can do again.

Maya asked Nell what she had tried so far and what she might try next, and she waited without rescuing her. The questions were small ones, but they turned the puzzle from a wall into a path and handed the thinking back to the child. A good teacher, she was discovering, spends a great deal more time asking questions than giving answers.

After a quarter of an hour of frowning and sorting, Nell found the piece that she had been missing, and the harbour was complete. She shouted that she had done it all by herself, and she was perfectly right, because Maya had given her nothing but questions. The pride in her face was of a kind that cannot be handed to a child by anybody else.

On Monday a large delivery went to the wrong town, and Colm called the whole team round a table. To Maya's surprise he did not search for somebody to blame but asked, in an even voice, what had happened and what the team could learn. The atmosphere in the room, which she had expected to be tense, was calm and almost curious.

Colm began by admitting that a mistake of his own had helped to cause the problem, and he described it plainly, without excuses. Once the manager had gone first, the others found it much easier to speak, and within minutes the team had traced the whole chain of small errors. Studies of workplaces suggest that teams who feel safe to admit mistakes often learn faster than those who hide them.

Dev suggested that the team write a short note after every large job, listing what had gone well and what they would change next time. It took only five minutes, and within a month the habit had become so ordinary that nobody remembered a time without it. Maya recognised it at once as the two lists in her notebook, grown up and moved into the office.

On a park bench, with Nell playing on the swings, Maya and Theo talked about how they had been taught at school, where marks had so often seemed to matter more than understanding. They agreed that parents have one small tool that costs nothing, which is to ask at the end of the day not what mark did you get but what was hard today, and what did you try. The question, they thought, invites a child to see difficulty as part of the process and not as a sign of failure.

In the cold, dark weeks of winter, Maya's motivation vanished once more, and this time it did not feel like a landing but like a draught under the door. Even the song she loved seemed a chore, and the guitar stayed on its stand for four evenings in a row. She remembered what Ines had said about feelings coming and going like weather, and she did not find it as comforting as she had hoped.

Maya made a small deal with herself, which was to sit down with the guitar for just two minutes and then to stop if she wished. On most evenings, once she had begun, she carried on for twenty, because starting is far harder than continuing. Motivation, she realised, often follows action and does not precede it, and routine is what gets you to the first note.

After a week of unusually long evenings, in which she was trying to catch up on the lost days, Maya's wrist began to ache. Ines told her firmly to stop and rest, since pain is a signal to be heeded and not a challenge to be beaten, and she added that a persistent ache is a matter for a doctor. Wanting to improve is admirable, but a body is not an unlimited resource, and it keeps its own accounts.

Theo reminded her, over tea, that effort is not unlimited magic, and he drew her a picture of a tall person and a short person standing beside a basketball hoop. No amount of training would give the shorter one the reach of the taller, he pointed out, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Nobody was disputing that effort matters; the question was merely whether it matters without limit.

Maya agreed that talent and starting points are real, and that genes play a part in many abilities, as the books she had read were honest enough to say. Even so, it is remarkably hard to know anyone's limit until they have practised well, with good teaching, for a long time, and most of us stop long before we reach it. The honest position was somewhere between the two stories, and it was less dramatic than either.

Maya came across the popular rule that ten thousand hours of practice will make anyone an expert, and she looked into where it had come from. It turned out to be a simplification of research that was more careful: the way you practise matters at least as much as the number of hours, and different fields demand very different amounts. There is no magic number, and no guarantee, that you will arrive when the clock runs out.

Maya also thought about luck, and the thought was a sobering one that she could not easily put aside. She had enough time, enough money for lessons, a good teacher two streets away and a family that did not laugh at her, and many people who wished to learn had none of those things. Effort is real, but it works inside circumstances that nobody chooses, and it would be unkind to forget it.

Ines told her, with typical frankness, that the research on mindset is mixed, and that its effects are often smaller than the popular books suggest. Believing that you can grow is a start, she said, but it is not a method, and it cannot replace good teaching, good strategies, support and the time to practise. The belief opens the door, and then you still have to walk through it.

Maya rubbed out a grand ambition that she had once scribbled on the card, in which she became a concert performer, and wrote a more honest one in its place. She wanted to play well enough to give her friends pleasure, to keep improving for as long as she lived and to enjoy every part of the journey. A goal that fits your life, she decided, is worth more than a fantasy that does not.

Maya understood at last that real limits do not make effort pointless, since they only mean that effort is not a magic spell. Nobody could tell her how far she would go, and she did not need to know, so she opened the case on that dark evening and played for two minutes, and then for twenty. The point of learning, she thought, was never to become someone else but to become more fully herself.

Early in February, a year after she had made it, Maya was scrolling through her phone when she came across an old file called Day 31. She had almost forgotten that it existed, and for a moment she hesitated, as one does before opening an old letter. Then she made a cup of tea, sat down by the window and pressed play.

The recording was every bit as bad as she remembered, with its late chords, its buzzing strings and a long, nervous silence in the middle. She could even hear her own held breath, and the sound of a person who did not believe in herself. Instead of wincing, she smiled warmly, because she knew precisely how much had happened since.

Maya propped her phone on the very same pile of books and recorded the same exercise as before, followed by The Water Is Wide. She did not hold her breath, she did not rush and when a small slip came in the middle of the song she simply carried on. The comparison was about to be made, and she found that she was not afraid of it.

She played the two recordings one after the other, and the difference was obvious without a single word of explanation. The buzz had gone, the timing was steady, the tone was warmer and the second player sounded like someone who expected to be listened to. A year of ordinary evenings, none of them remarkable, had added up to something that she could hear.

Maya turned the pages of her notebook, which had grown thick and crowded over the year, with its meadow drawing, its staircase and its long three-column list of mistakes. Nearly every entry now had a fix beside it and a small tick, and the dates told a story that no single evening could have told. The book was a map of a year of changing, drawn by the person who had changed.

At her next lesson Ines took out the worn page of beginner exercises that she had given Maya a year earlier, and it was now covered with Maya's own pencil marks. Every mark, Ines said, was a small struggle that had been met and won, and she hung the page proudly on the wall beside the others. Then she reached into her bag and produced a new page, a good deal harder than the last.

At a family dinner in Theo's house, Theo spoke Portuguese to Ana's mother for a full five minutes, with only three mistakes and a good deal of pride. She understood every word and answered with a smile so broad that it seemed to light the table, and Ana wiped her eyes. Afterwards Maya played The Water Is Wide, softly, while Nell hummed along somewhat out of tune.

On a park bench, Maya counted on her fingers what she would say to anyone who was starting something new. The brain keeps changing, a mistake is a piece of information, small steps beat vague wishes, slow and regular practice beats occasional heroics and rest is part of the work, as are good feedback and a little kindness towards yourself. She ran out of fingers long before she ran out of ideas, and she laughed at herself.

The same week Maya filled in a form for adult swimming lessons, an activity that she had avoided since she was small and had been told that she was hopeless at. She knew perfectly well that she would be bad at it at first, and the thought, which would once have frightened her, now made her smile. Everything that she had learned from the guitar was waiting, ready to be used again in the water.

The lesson Maya carried away was never really about the guitar, for the same truth applies to a language, a sport, a craft or a difficult job. Your mind is not a finished object but a living thing that keeps changing with attention, patience and good practice. Begin where you are, expect to make mistakes, learn from every one of them, and then do it all again tomorrow.
